title: Household measures: teaspoons to gallons
blurb: Convert teaspoons, tablespoons, fluid ounces, cups, pints, quarts and gallons in either direction, and handle the customary length and weight units that support them.
question: A patient drinks 1 pint 6 fl oz of water, 1.5 cups of juice and 14 fl oz of tea in one shift. How many quarts is that in total?

teach.h: Household measures: seven units, six factors
teach.body: Formally, household measures are the US customary units of liquid volume: teaspoon, tablespoon, fluid ounce, cup, pint, quart and gallon. Each is a fixed multiple of the one below it, but the multiples are 3, 2, 8, 2, 2 and 4, not powers of 10. In plain English: there is no decimal ladder to slide along, so you must know each factor by heart and multiply or divide by it. The HESI A2 expects these from memory.

teach.caption: Each arrow is its own factor: 3, 2, 8, 2, 2, 4. Multiply them along the chain for bigger jumps.

teach.caption: Build the right-hand column from the ladder rather than memorizing it blind: 1 cup = 8 fl oz × 2 = 16 tbsp.

teach.h: Big to small, multiply. Small to big, divide.
teach.body: One big unit holds several small ones, so changing to the SMALLER unit means MORE of them: multiply. Changing to a BIGGER unit means fewer: divide. To stay safe, write the factor as a fraction with the unit you want on top and the unit you are cancelling on the bottom. 40 fl oz × (1 cup / 8 fl oz) = 5 cups: the fluid ounces cancel, and the answer is in cups.

items: 2 qt to cups: 1 qt = 2 pt and 1 pt = 2 cups, so 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 cups. Check: 8 ÷ 2 ÷ 2 = 2 qt.
3/4 cup to tbsp: 1 cup = 16 tbsp, so 3/4 × 16 = 12 tbsp. Check: 12 ÷ 16 = 3/4.
1.5 gal to pints: 1 gal = 8 pt, so 1.5 × 8 = 12 pt. Check: 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5 gal.
48 fl oz to quarts: 1 qt = 32 fl oz, so 48 ÷ 32 = 1.5 qt. Check: 1.5 × 32 = 48 fl oz.
9 tsp to fl oz: 9 ÷ 3 = 3 tbsp, then 3 ÷ 2 = 1.5 fl oz. Check: 1.5 × 6 = 9 tsp.

teach.caption: Never mix them: a weight in ounces cannot be turned into cups without extra information.

teach.caption: Same rule: going to a smaller unit, multiply. 2 yd = 6 ft = 72 in; 3 lb = 48 oz.

teach.h: Scenario: DeShawn totals a patient's fluid intake
teach.body: DeShawn, a nursing assistant studying for the HESI A2, records 1 pint 6 fl oz of water, 1.5 cups of juice and 14 fl oz of tea. Convert everything to fluid ounces: 1 pint = 16 fl oz, so 16 + 6 = 22; 1.5 cups × 8 = 12; tea 14. Total: 22 + 12 + 14 = 48 fl oz. A quart is 32 fl oz, so 48 ÷ 32 = 1.5 qt. Check: 1.5 × 32 = 48.

teach.text: Household units are NOT decimal, and the classic slips are factor swaps: a cup is 8 fl oz (not 16, which is a pint), a quart is 4 cups (not 2, which is a pint), a gallon is 4 quarts (not 8), and 3 TEASPOONS make 1 tablespoon (not the reverse). If a question wants milliliters for a cup, pint, quart or gallon, it prints the factor: use that number.

items: Volume: 3 tsp = 1 tbsp; 2 tbsp = 1 fl oz; 8 fl oz = 1 cup; 2 cups = 1 pt; 2 pt = 1 qt; 4 qt = 1 gal.
Derived: 1 cup = 16 tbsp = 48 tsp; 1 qt = 32 fl oz; 1 gal = 16 cups = 128 fl oz.
To a smaller unit, multiply; to a bigger unit, divide. Put the wanted unit on top of the factor.
Mixed amounts: convert everything to the smallest unit, then work.
Support units: 12 in = 1 ft; 3 ft = 1 yd; 5,280 ft = 1 mi; 16 oz = 1 lb; 2,000 lb = 1 ton.

summary: You can now move up and down the household ladder from teaspoons to gallons, in one step or several, and total mixed liquid amounts. You can also convert the customary length and weight units that appear alongside them without falling into decimal thinking.

A.q: A hallway runner is 162 inches long. What is its length in yards?
A.why: 1 yd = 36 in, and inches to yards is small to big, so divide: 162 ÷ 36 = 4.5 yd. Check: 4.5 × 36 = 162 in.

whyNot.2: This divides by 10, as if customary units were decimal.
whyNot.3: This divides by 3, the feet-per-yard factor, but the starting unit is inches.

A.q: A bag of flour weighs 5 lb 4 oz. What is its weight in ounces?
A.why: 5 lb × 16 = 80 oz, plus the 4 oz: 80 + 4 = 84 oz. Check: 84 ÷ 16 = 5 remainder 4.

whyNot.2: This uses 12 oz per pound, the inches-per-foot factor (5 × 12 + 4).
whyNot.3: This converts the 5 lb but forgets to add the extra 4 oz.

A.q: A soup recipe calls for 3 quarts of broth. How many cups of broth is this?
A.why: 1 qt = 2 pt and 1 pt = 2 cups, so 1 qt = 4 cups. 3 × 4 = 12 cups. Check: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 qt.

whyNot.0: This treats a quart as 2 cups; that is a pint.
whyNot.1: This treats a quart as 8 cups.
whyNot.2: This uses 16 cups, the number of cups in a gallon, for each quart.

B.q: How many 1-cup servings are in 3 1/2 quarts of juice?
B.why: 1 qt = 2 pt = 4 cups, so 3.5 × 4 = 14 cups. Check: 14 ÷ 4 = 3.5 qt.

whyNot.0: This uses 2 cups per quart; 2 cups make a pint, and a quart is 4 cups.
whyNot.1: This converts 3 quarts (12 cups) and leaves out the extra half quart (2 cups).
whyNot.3: This uses 8 cups per quart; 1 qt = 2 pt = 4 cups.

B.q: A walking trail is 2.5 miles long. What is its length in feet?
B.why: 1 mi = 5,280 ft, and miles to feet is big to small, so multiply: 2.5 × 5,280 = 13,200 ft.

whyNot.2: This divides 5,280 by 2.5 instead of multiplying.
whyNot.3: This multiplies by 12 again, which gives inches, not feet.

B.q: How many teaspoons are in 1/4 cup?
B.why: 1/4 cup = 8 ÷ 4 = 2 fl oz. 2 fl oz × 2 = 4 tbsp. 4 tbsp × 3 = 12 tsp. Check: 1 cup = 48 tsp, and 48 ÷ 4 = 12.

whyNot.0: 4 is the number of tablespoons; the last step (× 3) is missing.
whyNot.2: This skips the fluid ounce to tablespoon step (2 fl oz × 3).
whyNot.3: This uses 16 fl oz per cup, which doubles every later step.

C.q: A patient drinks 1 pint 6 fl oz of water, 1.5 cups of juice and 14 fl oz of tea. What is the total intake in quarts?
C.why: In fluid ounces: 16 + 6 = 22; 1.5 × 8 = 12; 14. Total 48 fl oz. 1 qt = 32 fl oz, so 48 ÷ 32 = 1.5 qt.

whyNot.0: This divides by 16, treating a quart as 2 cups (that is a pint).
whyNot.1: This uses 16 fl oz per cup for the juice (24 fl oz), giving 60 ÷ 32.
whyNot.3: 48 ÷ 128 = 0.375 is the total in gallons, not quarts.

C.q: A clinic's water cooler jug holds 5 gallons. Staff fill 6-fl oz paper cups from it. How many full cups can be poured from one jug?
C.why: 1 gal = 128 fl oz, so 5 gal = 640 fl oz. 640 ÷ 6 = 106.67. Only full cups count, so 106.

whyNot.1: 640 ÷ 6 = 106.67, and the 107th cup would not be full, so round down.
whyNot.2: This divides 640 fl oz by 8, the size of a standard cup, instead of the 6-fl oz paper cup.
whyNot.3: This uses 16 fl oz per gallon (the pint value), so the jug looks like 80 fl oz.

C.q: A newborn weighed 7 lb 14 oz at birth and 9 lb 3 oz at four weeks. How much weight did the baby gain?
C.why: Borrow 1 lb = 16 oz: 9 lb 3 oz = 8 lb 19 oz. Then 19 - 14 = 5 oz and 8 - 7 = 1 lb. Check in ounces: 147 - 126 = 21 oz = 1 lb 5 oz.

whyNot.0: This borrows the pound but then subtracts the ounces backward (14 - 3 = 11).
whyNot.1: This borrows 12 oz instead of 16 (3 + 12 = 15, then 15 - 14 = 1).
whyNot.2: This subtracts smaller from larger in each column (9 - 7 and 14 - 3) without borrowing.

reteach.title: Think of packs and cases
reteach.question: A store sells soda in 12-can packs and 2-pack cases. How does counting cans show you when to multiply and when to divide?

blocks.body: If one pack holds 12 cans, then 3 packs hold 3 × 12 = 36 cans: opening big containers into small ones means multiplying. Packing 36 loose cans back into packs means dividing: 36 ÷ 12 = 3 packs. A gallon is just a "pack" of 4 quarts, a cup is a pack of 8 fluid ounces, and a tablespoon is a pack of 3 teaspoons. Ask yourself: am I unpacking (multiply) or packing up (divide)?

blocks.text: A pack size is never automatically 10. Ask how many small units are inside ONE big unit (3, 2, 8, 2, 2, 4) before you multiply or divide.

explain.body: 8 fl oz = 1 cup, 2 cups = 1 pt, 2 pt = 1 qt, 4 qt = 1 gal. So 1 gal = 8 pt = 16 cups = 128 fl oz.

test.q: How many pints are in 3 gallons?

whyNot.0: 12 is the number of quarts; each quart is 2 pints.
whyNot.2: This treats a gallon as 2 pints.
whyNot.3: 48 is the number of cups in 3 gallons.

explain.body: 3 tsp = 1 tbsp and 2 tbsp = 1 fl oz, so 1 fl oz = 6 tsp. A cup (8 fl oz) is 16 tbsp or 48 tsp.

test.q: How many tablespoons are in 1 1/2 cups?
test.why: 1 cup = 8 fl oz × 2 = 16 tbsp, so 1.5 × 16 = 24 tbsp.

whyNot.0: This counts 1 tablespoon per fluid ounce (8 per cup); 1 fl oz = 2 tbsp.
whyNot.1: This uses 16 fl oz per cup, the pint value, which doubles the answer.
whyNot.3: 72 is the number of teaspoons in 1 1/2 cups.

explain.body: 12 in = 1 ft, 3 ft = 1 yd (so 36 in = 1 yd), 5,280 ft = 1 mi. Yards to inches: multiply by 36, or by 3 and then 12.

test.q: A roll of medical tape is 15 yd long. What is its length in inches?
test.why: 15 yd × 36 in per yd = 540 in. (Or 15 × 3 = 45 ft, then 45 × 12 = 540 in.)

whyNot.0: This multiplies by 12, which is inches per foot, not per yard.
whyNot.1: 45 is the length in feet; the step to inches is missing.
whyNot.3: This divides 15 by 12 instead of multiplying.

explain.body: 16 oz = 1 lb and 2,000 lb = 1 ton. Pounds to ounces: multiply by 16. Weight ounces (oz) are not fluid ounces (fl oz).

test.q: A patient lost 2.25 lb during a hospital stay. How many ounces is this?
test.why: Pounds to ounces is big to small: 2.25 × 16 = 36 oz.

whyNot.3: This divides by 16 instead of multiplying.
